caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 식당, 구독형 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 손익계산서는 정해진 기간 동안 매출이 비용을 하나씩 거쳐 이익으로 내려가는 이야기다. 위에서 아래로, 기간을 정해서 읽는다.
misconception: 매출이 크거나 통장 잔고가 늘었으면 장사가 잘된 것이다.

sources.text: 재무회계의 표준 개념 (손익계산서, 매출·비용·이익, 기간 단위 보고)

factChecks.note: 'top line', 'bottom line'이 손익계산서의 맨 윗줄과 맨 아랫줄에서 온 표현이라는 설명은 일반적으로 알려진 용례입니다. 게시 전 사전으로 한 번 더 확인하세요.

cards.title: Where did March's $40,000 go?
body: Maya runs a neighborhood restaurant. At the end of March she tells a friend, "We did $40,000 this month."
Her friend asks a simple follow-up: "And how much did you keep?" Maya isn't sure. The answer lives on one page most owners rarely read.

image.label: Restaurant owner looking at a long receipt at closing time
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 영업이 끝난 작은 식당 카운터에서 주인이 바닥까지 늘어진 긴 영수증을 들고 고개를 갸웃함. 영수증 맨 위에 "$40,000", 맨 아래는 물음표. 실제 상표나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Was March a good month?
body: Maya wants a fair answer to one question: did the restaurant make money in March?

options.text: March sales compared with February sales
options.feedback: Sales show how busy she was, not what she kept. A busier month can still lose money if costs grew faster.

options.text: How much the bank balance rose during March
options.feedback: Close, and easy to check. But the bank balance also moves with loans, late bills and payments that belong to other months.

options.text: March sales minus every March cost, line by line
options.feedback: This answers the question directly and shows where the money went. That page has a name, coming up next.

cards.title: Maya's March, top to bottom.
body: Read it like a waterfall. Each line takes a share of the $40,000 until only **$5,000** is left.

breakdown.label: Revenue
breakdown.detail: Everything customers paid for meals and drinks

cards.softwareNote: A software company's page looks the same. Revenue at the top is subscriptions. Costs are hosting, support, salaries and marketing. Different lines, same waterfall.

cards.title: The income statement
body: The **income statement**, also called the *profit and loss* or P&L, lists a business's revenue and costs for a set period and ends with its profit or loss.
Revenue sits at the top, which is why people call sales the *top line*. Profit sits at the bottom: the *bottom line*.
Maya's $40,000 was the top line. Her friend was asking about the bottom line.

image.label: A one-page statement with the top and bottom lines highlighted
image.brief: 종이 한 장 형태의 손익계산서 일러스트. 맨 윗줄 "Revenue"와 맨 아랫줄 "Profit"에 각각 형광펜 강조와 "Top line", "Bottom line" 말풍선. 가운데 비용 줄들은 흐리게.

cards.title: A movie, not a photo.
body: An income statement always covers a stretch of time: a month, a quarter or a year. "Profit of $5,000" means nothing until you know *for which period*.
That's what makes it useful. You can line up March against February, or this March against last March, and see which lines moved.
Other reports work differently. The balance sheet, coming next, is a photo of a single day.

cards.title: Same shape, any business.
body: The lines change by industry. The order stays the same.
list: **Plumber:** call-out fees, minus parts, van, fuel and wages
**Small factory:** product sales, minus materials, labor, machines and rent
**Hotel:** room nights, minus cleaning, staff, energy and booking fees
cards.callout: Start at what came in. Subtract what it took. Read what's left.

cards.title: It isn't your bank account.
body: The income statement counts sales when they're earned and costs when they're used, not when cash moves. A profitable month can still leave the account short, for example when a big supplier bill lands.
One month can also mislead. A slow season or a once-a-year repair can swing the bottom line. Compare the same periods, and look at several in a row before deciding.

cards.title: Now it's a subscription app.
body: Revenue grew from $100k in Q1 to $130k in Q2. Yet profit went from +$20k to −$10k.
The cost lines: hosting $10k → $13k, salaries $50k → $60k, marketing $20k → $67k. Where do you look first?

options.text: Nowhere yet. Revenue grew 30%, so the loss is just a growing pain
options.feedback: You keep the growth story but skip the page that explains the loss. Growth only helps if costs don't outrun it.

options.text: Marketing. It more than tripled, so ask what it bought
options.feedback: Hosting and salaries grew no faster than revenue. Marketing explains almost the whole swing, so that's where the real question is.

options.text: Salaries. They're the biggest line, so start there
options.feedback: Big lines matter, but salaries grew only 20%, slower than revenue. Reading what *changed* beats reading what's largest.

cards.title: Read it top to bottom, for a set period.
body: The income statement tells you whether a period's work made money, and where the money went on the way down.
**Try it today:** write last month's revenue at the top of a page. List your five biggest costs below it and subtract. Is what's left what you expected?
